summary:
# ORBIT: Project Summary

**ORBIT (Orbital Real-time Biomedical & Telemetry)** is an offline-first health monitoring tool for astronauts on long-duration missions, built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

**The Problem.** Communication delays mean deep-space crews cannot rely on real-time flight surgeons. Radiation, isolation, gravity changes, and closed environments pose severe health risks.

**What ORBIT Does.** It tracks health indicators (heart rate, blood pressure, radiation, CO₂, sleep debt) using a rule engine. Alerts require three confirming samples to prevent false alarms. If issues appear, ORBIT prompts check-ins and escalates if responses indicate distress or are missing.

**Key Features**
- 3D digital twin & interactive anatomy view
- Live dashboard with dynamic charts & color codes
- Explainable rule engine showing triggers & actions
- Crew check-in with automatic escalation
- Optional local AI (Ollama) for explanations (rules take over when off)
- Offline-first: local data queuing, sync, & STALE tracking
- Gamified health tasks, medical guide, multi-crew support & mission environments
- Mission event history for post-mission reviews

**Technology.** FastAPI, Python, SQLite, WebSocket, Next.js, React, and Docker.

**Safety Notice.** Uses synthetic demo data. ORBIT supports decisions; it does not diagnose.

*When Earth is far, your data keeps you close.*
details:
ORBIT (Orbital Real-time Biomedical & Telemetry) is an offline-first health monitoring and decision-support tool that helps astronauts assess their own health during long-duration missions.

WHAT IT DOES

On missions to the Moon and Mars, communication delays mean the crew cannot always rely on flight surgeons in real time. ORBIT collects health and environment indicators (heart rate, blood pressure, radiation dose, cabin CO2 and sleep debt), evaluates them with a transparent rule engine, and tells the astronaut what is happening, why an alert was raised and what to do next. Status is color-coded (normal, warning, critical, stale) so it can be read at a glance.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Telemetry (from sensors or a clearly labelled simulator) is validated and stored locally.

2. NumPy and Pandas calculate trends, variability and cumulative radiation dose.

3. A deterministic risk engine classifies each reading. A status changes only after three consecutive confirming samples, so a single sensor spike does not cause a false alarm.

4. When a concerning pattern appears, ORBIT asks the crew member to check in. An "OK" answer is recorded; a "need help" answer or no answer at all triggers escalation. A missing response never clears an alert.

5. Results are pushed live through WebSocket to a dashboard with dynamic charts, an interactive anatomy view where each body system can be clicked to see its function and status, and a 3D digital twin.

6. An optional local AI assistant (Ollama, pre-downloaded) explains findings in plain language. It never decides risk. If it is switched off, rule-based explanations take over, so core monitoring works without internet or AI.

7. If the data stream stops, the state becomes STALE instead of normal. Readings are queued locally and synced to the ground when the link returns.

Additional features include a medical guide that explains measurements and risks in simple language, daily health tasks with points and streaks to keep the crew engaged, multi-crew support, switchable mission environments, notes, search, and a full event history for post-mission review by medical staff.

BENEFITS

- Helps astronauts who are not medical experts understand their health status and act early.

- Works without internet, which matches real deep-space conditions.

- Every alert is explainable and auditable: the rule, the value and the recommended action are always shown.

- Safety-first design: AI explains, rules decide.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Python, FastAPI, NumPy, Pandas, SQLite, WebSocket, Ollama (optional local LLM), Next.js, React, TypeScript, Recharts, Framer Motion, Tailwind CSS, Docker and pytest.

NASA RESOURCES

We used NASA's Human Research Program framework of the five hazards of human spaceflight (space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile closed environments) to choose which indicators to monitor and to structure the medical guide.

IMPORTANT NOTES

All demonstration data is synthetic. Thresholds are demonstration values and must be reviewed by medical and spaceflight experts before any real use. ORBIT supports decisions; it does not diagnose.
dataRefs: Resurs: NASA HRP Human Health and Performance / Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight (Space radiation, isolation/confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, hostile closed environments).
